 Order
The present petition was disposed of by this Court on March 19, 2018, whereby this Court has declared that the petitioner is entitled to the benefit of Section 24(2) of the Act of 2013.

The said judgment was challenged by the Delhi Development Authority, the respondent no. 3 in Civil Appeal No. 7678/2021, which was decided by the Supreme Court by passing the following order:-
"This appeal takes exception to the judgment and order dated 19.3.2018 passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in Writ Petition (C) No.2786 of 2015, whereby the High Court declared that the acquisition proceedings in respect of subject J.and had lapsed in light of Section ^24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act,2013.
According to the appellant, possession of the land bearing Khasra No.53/18 has been duly taken and handed over to the Delhi Development Authority.

however, noted that the physical possession was taken only in respect of 3 Bigha 16 Biswas of the larger area acquired under the concerned notification.
This finding is countered by the appellant(s).

sentences.text: It is further urged by the learned counsel for the appellant that in any case, the compensation amount has been offered to the landowners for the entire area as asserted in paragraph 9 of the affidavit filed before the High Court to oppose the writ petition.
Despite that, the High Court proceeded to find in paragraph 9 of the impugned judgment that compensation in respect of entire area of subject land has not been paid to the writ petitioner(s).
Be it noted, the High Court essentially decided the case by following the decision of this Court in Government (NCT of Delhi) vs. Manav Dharam Trust & Anr., (2017) 6 see 751.

All contentions available to both sides be decided by the High court on its own merits and in accordance with law including by taking into account the latest decision of the constitution Bench of this Court, referred to above.
All contentions available to both parties are left open.
The parties to appear before the High Court on 08.02.2022.
The High court may set down the matter for hearing as per its convenience.
However, we request the High Court to expeditiously dispose of the writ petition.
The appeal and pending applications stand disposed of in the above terms."

(emphasis supplied).
2. A perusal of the same reveal that the Supreme Court has set aside the judgment dated March 19,
2018 passed in the Writ Petition and remanded the matter back to this Court, for a fresh decision in accordance with law including taking into account the latest decision of the Constitution Bench.
The Supreme Court left open all contentions available to both the parties.

3. The petition has been filed with the following prayers:
"i. Issue an appropriate writ, order or directions declaring the entire acquisition proceedings in respect of the land admeasuring 50 square yards comprised in plot No. 1067 Khasra no 53/18 situated in the revenue estate of Village Karala, Tirthankar Nagar, Jain Colony, Delhi, including the notification bearing no.

ii. Pass any further order/s that this Hon'ble Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the present case."

sentences.text:
4. At the outset, Mr. Sanjay Poddar, learned Senior Advocate appearing for Delhi Development Authority, respondent no. 3, has taken a plea that in view of the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Shiv Kumar vs. Union of India, (2019) 10 SCC 229, the petitioner being a purchaser through registered GPA, after the issuance of notifications under Section 4 & 6, of a land admeasuring 50 sq. yds. in Khasra No. 53/18, situated in the revenue estate of Village Karala,
Tirthankar Nagar, Jain Colony, Delhi, the petitioner has no locus to seek a prayer as sought in the petition i.e. seeking the benefit of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act.
5.

entities.text: Shiv Kumar vs. Union of India, (2019) 10 SCC 229
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This submission of Mr. Poddar has not been seriously contested by learned counsel for the petitioner.

We also find that the petitioner has stated in the petition that he had purchased the land admeasuring 50 sq. yds. comprising in Khasra no. 53/18, situated in Village Karala on November 25,
2005, which is after the Notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, issued on March 21, 2003 and a notification under Section 6 dated March 18, 2004 6.

The Supreme Court in Shiv Kumar (supra), more specifically paras 20, 21 & 29, has stated as under:
"20.
Given that, the transaction of sale, effected after section 4 notification, is void, is ineffective to transfer the land, such incumbents cannot invoke the provisions of section 24.

As the sale transaction did not clothe them with the title when the purchase was made; they cannot claim "possession" and challenge the acquisition as having lapsed under section 24 by questioning the legality or regularity of proceedings of taking over of possession under the 1894 Act.
It would be unfair and profoundly unjust and against the policy of the law to permit such a person to claim resettlement or claim the land back as envisaged under the Act of 2013.
When he has not been deprived of his livelihood but is a purchaser under a void transaction, the outcome of exploitative tactics played upon poor farmers who were unable to defend themselves.

21. Thus, under the provisions of Section 24 of the 2013 Act, challenge to acquisition proceeding of the taking over of possession under the 1894 Act cannot be made,
based on a void transaction nor declaration can be sought under section 24(2) by such incumbents to obtain the land.

The declaration that acquisition has lapsed under the 2013 Act is to get the property back whereas, the transaction once void, is always a void transaction, as no title can be acquired in the land as such no such declaration can be sought.

It would not be legal, just and equitable to give the land back to purchaser as land was not capable of being sold which was in process of Onkar Chand vs Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi And Ors on 19 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/74899335/
3 acquisition under the 1894 Act.

sentences.text: The 2013 Act does not confer any right on purchaser whose sale is ab initio void.
Such void transactions are not validated under the 2013 Act.
No rights are conferred by the provisions contained in the 2013 Act on such a purchaser as against the State.
xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx 29.
Concerning the illegal colony, averments have been made that the colony is an unauthorized and provisional order was passed to regularise it.
The plea taken is contradictory and shows the falsity of the claim raised by the purchasers.

That apart predecessors of the purchaser obtained the land based on power-of-attorney,
agreement to sell, and Will on 9.12.1982.
As per averments made in the writ application, Bijender Singh, who was owning  share, sold the share to Satya Narain by the documents like Agreement to Sell, Power of Attorney, or Will.
It has also been averred that Om Prakash sold the remaining  share to Satya Narain on 11.3.1984 by way of Agreement to Sale, Power of Attorney, or Will.

The purchase made through Agreement to Sale, Power of Attorney, or Will by Satya Narain did not confer a title upon him to transfer it to the purchasers apart from the fact that it was void in view of purchase after Section 4.
Based on purchase made from such owners whose title was not perfect, purchasers had no derivative title in the eye of law.
There was no legally recognized title deed in favor of Satya Narain."

7. That apart the Supreme Court in its latest opinion in the case of State of Haryana & Ors. vs.
Sushila & Ors., Civil Appeal No. 9205/2022, decided on January 13, 2023, has reiterated the same view in paras 4 & 4.1 as under:-
"4. Even otherwise as observed and held by this Court in the case of Delhi Administration Through Secretary, Land and Building vs. Pawan Kumar & Ors., Civil Appeal No.3646 of 2022 and Delhi Development Authority versus Godfrey Phillips (I) Ltd. & Ors, Civil Appeal No.3073 of 2022, the subsequent purchasers have no locus to challenge the acquisition and/or lapsing of acquisition.
4.1. Applying the law laid down by this Court in the aforesaid two decisions, the writ petition at the instance of the private respondents herein-original writ petitioners being subsequent purchasers ought not to have been entertained by the High Court challenging the acquisition proceedings and/or praying for lapse of the acquisition under Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013.

8. The aforesaid being the position of law, the petitioner is not entitled to the relief as prayed for.
The Writ Petition is dismissed.
